JSON: Name: disentangled_edge_restoration_ad Title: Disentangled anatomy learning and edge-to-image restoration for unsupervised anomaly detection in brain MRI Short Hypothesis: A model that (1) disentangles imaging-specific representations from imaging-invariant anatomical representations and (2) reconstructs pseudo-healthy images by restoring anatomical codes from anatomical edges will produce statistically significant improvements in voxel-level anomaly detection (higher AP and DSC) on multi-modality, multi-center brain MRI compared to conventional image-to-image reconstruction baselines trained on the same normal data. Related Work: Existing unsupervised brain MRI anomaly-detection approaches fall into three families: (1) self-supervised methods that synthesize anomalies and train discriminative detectors, which perform well on synthetic-like anomalies but generalize poorly to diverse real pathologies; (2) deep feature embedding approaches that measure distance in learned feature spaces (teacher–student, patch memory banks), which improve robustness but often lose fine-grained spatial detail and struggle with small lesions; and (3) reconstruction-based generative methods (autoencoders, VAE, GAN, diffusion models and recent two-stage inpainting pipelines) that detect anomalies via image reconstruction errors. Reconstruction methods can suppress anomalies if the generative model learns the normal manifold, but they typically (i) overfit imaging-specific cues from the training normal set (reducing cross-sequence and multi-center generalizability), (ii) propagate abnormal residuals from input to reconstruction when reconstructing directly from full images, and (iii) trade off anomaly suppression against preservation of personalized normal details, producing blurred or incomplete restorations. Prior disentanglement attempts improve invariance but suffer from unstable binarization/activation and modality leakage. No prior method combines stable anatomy–modality disentanglement with an edge-driven restoration that explicitly minimizes abnormal input pixels during reconstruction. Abstract: We address unsupervised voxel-level anomaly detection in multi-sequence, multi-center brain MRI by introducing a reconstruction framework that separates imaging-specific factors from imaging-invariant anatomy and restores pseudo-healthy images from anatomical edges. The method comprises two modules: (1) a disentangled representation module that decouples each MRI into a non-spatial modality vector and a spatial anatomical image using anatomy priors and a differentiable one-hot encoding to stabilize binarization; and (2) an edge-to-image restoration module that reconstructs an abstract anatomical code from anatomical edges and then recouples modality features via multi-level adaptive layers to produce high-fidelity pseudo-healthy images. Training is performed jointly on paired normal T1/T2 scans to align anatomical codes across sequences while preserving personalized modality information. The approach reduces anomalous residuals in reconstructions by design (edge-only restoration) and focuses reconstruction capacity on anatomy, improving detection generalizability across sequences and centers. Expected outcomes are higher voxel-level detection AP and DSC, reduced false positives from modality mismatch, and improved reconstruction fidelity of normal regions. Experiments: Datasets: Train on paired normal T1/T2 scans from IXI (N=577). Evaluate on nine public datasets totaling 4,443 subjects across pathologies and centers: BraTS-GLI, UPenn-GBM, UCSF-PDGM, BraTS-SSA, BraTS-PED, BraTS-MEN, BraTS-MET, MSLUB (MS), ATLAS (stroke). Preprocessing: RAI orientation, N4 bias correction, rigid registration to atlas, skull-stripping, intensity histogram matching to IXI, resample/crop to 112x160x112 for training. Baselines: representative methods from three categories: SSL (DRAEM, FPI), deep-feature (PatchCore, EfficientAD, MKD, RD4AD, UTRAD, AMCons), and reconstruction (AE, VAE, MemAE, RIAD, ProxyAno, AnoDDPM, AutoDDPM, PHANES, DAE). Metrics: voxel-level average precision (AUPRC), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) after greedy threshold search per dataset, reconstruction metrics (l1-REN, l1-REA, l1-ratio), and SSIM between input and reconstructed images. Training setup: Adam lr=1e-4, 150 epochs, batch size=2 (T1+T2 pairs from two subjects per batch), mixed precision, trained on two 24GB GPUs. Primary evaluation: compare AP and DSC per dataset and pooled across T1, T2, and combined. Statistical test: paired bootstrap or Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-subject AP and DSC between proposed and each baseline (report p-values). Ablation studies: (A) remove disentangled representation module (train edge-to-image restoration without anatomy binarization and one-hot encoding), (B) remove edge-to-image restoration (reconstruct PHI directly from anatomy image), (C) disable modality reuse (no multi-level adaptive layers), (D) remove anatomy-code consistency loss, (E) replace hybrid anomaly score with L1-only and SSIM-only scores, (F) vary post-processing minimum and mean filter kernel sizes in {0,3,5,7,9,11,13,15}. Additional experiments: - Train on homogeneous HCP young-adult normal dataset (~1,113 subjects) versus heterogeneous IXI to quantify training-data diversity effect on cross-center generalization. - Measure sensitivity to small lesions: evaluate per-lesion-size bins (e.g., <1cm3, 1–5cm3, >5cm3) for AP/DSC. Computational profiling: report GPU hours, peak memory, and inference throughput (slices/sec). Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Training data requirement: the method is designed for paired normal scans (e.g., T1/T2); absence of paired modalities or limited normal sample diversity may reduce disentanglement quality and generalization. 2) Anatomical deformation: large-scale pathological anatomical deformations (mass effect, tissue displacement, atrophy) may be preserved in anatomical edges, yielding pseudo-healthy reconstructions that retain structural deformation and causing false negatives. 3) Edge-only restoration blind spots: restoring from edges may omit subtle intensity/textural anomalies that are not well represented by high-frequency edges. 4) Binarization/stability: differentiable one-hot encoding and binarization may still suffer activation failures or sensitivity to hyperparameters, degrading disentanglement and downstream detection. 5) Hyperparameter sensitivity and post-processing: detection depends on loss weight choices and post-processing filter sizes; greedy threshold search during evaluation may overestimate real-world performance. 6) Computational cost and scalability: training 3D joint models with multi-level adaptive layers and diffusion-like restorers requires substantial GPU memory and time, limiting rapid retraining for new sequences or larger datasets. 7) Dataset and label bias: public datasets vary in acquisition quality and annotation protocols; evaluation results may be biased by lesion-type prevalence, lesion sizes, or labeling quality. 8) Generalization to unseen sequences: incorporating new sequences (e.g., FLAIR) requires retraining or additional paired normal data; zero-shot generalization to arbitrary sequences is not guaranteed.
